lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: A filing system treats each part of a dotted code as a separate integer subcode and files in ascending order. Which code comes first: $12.05$, $12.1$, or $12.008$?
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The former statement is now a question. Its comparison and answer appear only in the numbered solution.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: Arrange March $15$, $2024$; January $20$, $2024$; November $5$, $2023$; and February $10$, $2025$ from oldest to newest.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: All date numbers in the chronological question are now enclosed in inline math.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: Compare the next subcodes as whole numbers: $5$, $1$, and $8$.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The dotted codes and all numeric prose in their worked example use inline math rather than code spans.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: Compare complete dates in this format from left to right.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The long lexicographic sentence is replaced by short statements about the order of date parts.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: A period or hyphen inside a code may separate parts. It may not be a math sign.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The stacked abstract terms are replaced with plain wording and separately defined code rules.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: 1. Add ending zeros so all entries show the same number of decimal places.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The decimal example has numbered steps and separate displayed padding equalities and a comparison.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: The year digits come before the month digits. The day digits decide the order only if the year and month match.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: Lexicographic terminology is removed. The lesson explains left-to-right comparison directly.

reasoning-clerical-ability#21.quote: The fixed date format **YYYY-MM-DD** puts the year first, the month second, and the day last.
reasoning-clerical-ability#21.note: The components and digit widths are explained, and Example 4 applies year-first date ordering.

reasoning-clerical-ability#24.quote: The next characters are $1$ and $2$. Since $1$ comes before $2$, $\text{A-10}$ comes first.
reasoning-clerical-ability#24.note: Core Concept teaches single-character comparison. Example 7 applies it to codes with unequal digit counts.

reasoning-clerical-ability#25.quote: Compare the last parts as whole numbers. Since $7$ is smaller than $12$, $\text{AB-5-7}$ comes first.
reasoning-clerical-ability#25.note: Example 8 applies the whole-number-part rule after matching the earlier hyphen-separated parts.

reasoning-clerical-ability#26.quote: A filing system compares the rightmost group first, then the middle group, then the leftmost group.
reasoning-clerical-ability#26.note: The terminal-digit procedure is taught locally and Example 9 applies every comparison group.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: Arrange $0452$, $0389$, $0401$, and $0395$ from smallest to largest.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: Arrange remains unglossed. The brief explicitly rules that this everyday instruction needs no definition.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: The dot separates parts here. It is not a decimal point under this rule.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: The optional Speed Tricks section is absent. The lesson follows the reduced Reasoning layout.

lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.quote: Place these records in reverse chronological order: July $8$, $2024$; July $21$, $2024$; and June $30$, $2024$.
lesson-clerical-ability-numeric-and-chro.note: A separate reverse chronological example now works through month and day comparisons.
